topic: HTN: BP goal <130/80 and first-line classes (thiazide, ACEi/ARB, CCB)
front: Newly diagnosed BP 148/94, no comorbidities. Start meds? Which classes, and what goal?
bottom: Yes: two first-line drugs, ideally one pill; goal <130/80.

bullets.clue: Drugs at ≥140/90, or ≥130/80 with CVD, diabetes, CKD or PREVENT risk ≥7.5%.
bullets.treat: Thiazide-type, dihydropyridine CCB, ACEi or ARB. Stage 2: two drugs, ideally one pill.
bullets.trap: Stage 2 (≥140/90) starts with two drugs; never combine an ACEi with an ARB.

back: Yes: two first-line drugs, ideally one pill; goal <130/80. Key clue: Drugs at ≥140/90, or ≥130/80 with CVD, diabetes, CKD or PREVENT risk ≥7.5%. Pharmacist move: Thiazide-type, dihydropyridine CCB, ACEi or ARB. Stage 2: two drugs, ideally one pill. Exam trap: Stage 2 (≥140/90) starts with two drugs; never combine an ACEi with an ARB.

source.recommendation: 2025 AHA/ACC High Blood Pressure guideline: goal <130/80; start medication at ≥140/90, or ≥130/80 with clinical CVD, diabetes, CKD or PREVENT 10-y risk ≥7.5%; first-line thiazide-type diuretic, long-acting DHP CCB, ACEi or ARB; stage 2: two first-line agents of different classes, preferably single-pill combination; avoid combined ACEi + ARB.

topic: Hypertensive emergency vs urgency: IV agents and 25% reduction
front: BP 220/130 with chest pain and confusion. Which drugs, and how fast do you lower it?
bottom: Hypertensive emergency: IV titratable agent.

bullets.clue: Organ damage defines emergency; no damage = urgency, treat orally.
bullets.treat: IV nicardipine, clevidipine, labetalol or esmolol; lower ≤25% in the first hour.
bullets.trap: Aortic dissection is the exception: SBP <120 within 20 minutes.

back: Hypertensive emergency: IV titratable agent. Key clue: Organ damage defines emergency; no damage = urgency, treat orally. Pharmacist move: IV nicardipine, clevidipine, labetalol or esmolol; lower ≤25% in the first hour. Exam trap: Aortic dissection is the exception: SBP <120 within 20 minutes.

source.recommendation: 2025 AHA/ACC High Blood Pressure guideline: hypertensive emergency with acute target-organ damage—ICU, IV titratable agents (e.g., nicardipine, clevidipine, labetalol, esmolol); reduce SBP by no more than 25% in the first hour, then to 160/100 over 2–6 h, then normal over 24–48 h; compelling conditions (aortic dissection) require SBP <120 within the first hour.

topic: Compelling indications: CKD w/ albuminuria, HFrEF, post-MI
front: Hypertension plus CKD with albuminuria, HFrEF, or recent MI. Which drug classes?
bottom: Match the drug to the compelling indication.

bullets.clue: CKD with albuminuria: ACEi or ARB, titrated to max tolerated.
bullets.treat: HFrEF: GDMT (ARNI/ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i). Post-MI: beta-blocker plus ACEi/ARB.
bullets.trap: Check potassium and creatinine 2–4 weeks after starting a RAS inhibitor.

back: Match the drug to the compelling indication. Key clue: CKD with albuminuria: ACEi or ARB, titrated to max tolerated. Pharmacist move: HFrEF: GDMT (ARNI/ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i). Post-MI: beta-blocker plus ACEi/ARB. Exam trap: Check potassium and creatinine 2–4 weeks after starting a RAS inhibitor.

source.recommendation: 2025 AHA/ACC HTN guideline: compelling indications guide drug choice (CKD with albuminuria—ACEi/ARB; HFrEF—GDMT; post-MI—beta-blocker and ACEi/ARB). KDIGO 2024 CKD: RASi titrated to maximum tolerated dose for CKD with albuminuria; monitor BP, creatinine and potassium within 2–4 weeks of starting or changing dose.

topic: HFrEF GDMT four pillars & titration (ARNI, BB, MRA, SGLT2i)
front: New HFrEF (EF 30%). What are the four pillars, and how fast do you start them?
bottom: ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor.

bullets.clue: Start all four quickly; order is flexible; titrate to target doses.
bullets.treat: Switching ACEi to sacubitril/valsartan: 36-hour washout.
bullets.trap: Beta-blocker must be carvedilol, metoprolol succinate or bisoprolol.

back: ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor. Key clue: Start all four quickly; order is flexible; titrate to target doses. Pharmacist move: Switching ACEi to sacubitril/valsartan: 36-hour washout. Exam trap: Beta-blocker must be carvedilol, metoprolol succinate or bisoprolol.

diagram.alt: HFrEF four pillars started together in any order: ARNI (or ACE inhibitor or ARB), evidence-based beta-blocker (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol), MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor. 36-hour washout from ACE inhibitor before ARNI.

source.recommendation: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline: HFrEF GDMT—ARNI (or ACEi/ARB), evidence-based beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i (COR 1); ARNI not within 36 h of last ACEi dose. 2024 ACC Expert Consensus Decision Pathway for HFrEF: initiate GDMT rapidly, sequence flexible, titrate to target doses.

topic: HFrEF drugs to avoid (non-DHP CCB, TZDs, NSAIDs)
front: Patient with HFrEF gets diltiazem, pioglitazone and naproxen. Which ones worsen HF?
bottom: All three: avoid in HFrEF.

bullets.clue: Non-DHP CCBs, thiazolidinediones, NSAIDs.
bullets.treat: Also avoid cilostazol, dronedarone and class IC antiarrhythmics.
bullets.trap: Amlodipine is neutral and OK for BP or angina.

back: All three: avoid in HFrEF. Key clue: Non-DHP CCBs, thiazolidinediones, NSAIDs. Pharmacist move: Also avoid cilostazol, dronedarone and class IC antiarrhythmics. Exam trap: Amlodipine is neutral and OK for BP or angina.

source.recommendation: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline: in HFrEF, non-DHP calcium channel blockers, thiazolidinediones, NSAIDs, dronedarone and class IC antiarrhythmics are harmful; cilostazol labeling contraindicates use in HF. Amlodipine is neutral.

topic: Acute decompensated HF: IV loop diuretic dosing
front: Admitted for decompensated HF on furosemide 40 mg PO daily. First IV loop dose?
bottom: IV dose equal to or above the home oral dose.

bullets.clue: Per guideline, the IV dose should equal or exceed the total daily oral dose.
bullets.treat: Give IV furosemide at least 40 mg; titrate to urine output and symptoms.
bullets.trap: Equivalents: furosemide 40 PO = torsemide 20 = bumetanide 1.

back: IV dose equal to or above the home oral dose. Key clue: Per guideline, the IV dose should equal or exceed the total daily oral dose. Pharmacist move: Give IV furosemide at least 40 mg; titrate to urine output and symptoms. Exam trap: Equivalents: furosemide 40 PO = torsemide 20 = bumetanide 1.

source.recommendation: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline: in hospitalized HF with congestion, IV loop diuretics promptly; initial IV dose should equal or exceed chronic oral daily dose, then adjust to response. Loop equivalence per labeling/standard references.

topic: ASCVD/dyslipidemia: statin intensity, LDL-C goals, add-on ezetimibe/PCSK9i, Lp(a)
front: Patient with recent MI and LDL-C 90 on max statin. What's the 2026 target, and what's next?
bottom: Very high risk: LDL-C <55 mg/dL.

bullets.clue: Other ASCVD: LDL-C <70. Measure Lp(a) once in every adult.
bullets.treat: Add ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor if still above goal.
bullets.trap: Lp(a) ≥125 nmol/L (50 mg/dL) is a risk enhancer.

back: Very high risk: LDL-C <55 mg/dL. Key clue: Other ASCVD: LDL-C <70. Measure Lp(a) once in every adult. Pharmacist move: Add ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor if still above goal. Exam trap: Lp(a) ≥125 nmol/L (50 mg/dL) is a risk enhancer.

source.recommendation: 2026 ACC/AHA multisociety Dyslipidemia guideline (replaces 2018): very-high-risk secondary prevention LDL-C goal <55 mg/dL (non-HDL-C <85); other ASCVD generally <70 mg/dL; add nonstatin therapy (ezetimibe, PCSK9 mAb) when above goal on maximally tolerated statin; measure Lp(a) at least once in all adults; Lp(a) ≥125 nmol/L (50 mg/dL) is a risk enhancer.

topic: ACS: DAPT, P2Y12 choice, duration
front: NSTEMI going to PCI. Which P2Y12 inhibitor, aspirin dose, and DAPT length?
bottom: Ticagrelor or prasugrel over clopidogrel; aspirin 81 mg.

bullets.clue: DAPT usually 12 months; selected patients can drop aspirin after 1 month on ticagrelor.
bullets.treat: Prasugrel: contraindicated after stroke or TIA; generally avoid ≥75; <60 kg consider 5 mg daily.
bullets.trap: Aspirin >100 mg reduces ticagrelor's benefit.

back: Ticagrelor or prasugrel over clopidogrel; aspirin 81 mg. Key clue: DAPT usually 12 months; selected patients can drop aspirin after 1 month on ticagrelor. Pharmacist move: Prasugrel: contraindicated after stroke or TIA; generally avoid ≥75; <60 kg consider 5 mg daily. Exam trap: Aspirin >100 mg reduces ticagrelor's benefit.

source.recommendation: 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline: ticagrelor or prasugrel preferred over clopidogrel with PCI; DAPT 12 months default; transition to ticagrelor monotherapy after ≥1 month reasonable in selected patients to reduce bleeding; aspirin 75–100 mg maintenance; prasugrel contraindicated with prior stroke/TIA. Ticagrelor labeling: aspirin maintenance >100 mg reduces effectiveness.

topic: STEMI fibrinolysis contraindications
front: STEMI, PCI more than 2 hours away. Which patients can't get a fibrinolytic?
bottom: Absolute: prior ICH, recent stroke, active bleeding, dissection.

bullets.clue: Ischemic stroke or significant head trauma within 3 months; intracranial tumor.
bullets.treat: If eligible, give the lytic within 30 minutes of arrival.
bullets.trap: BP >180/110 is relative, not absolute.

back: Absolute: prior ICH, recent stroke, active bleeding, dissection. Key clue: Ischemic stroke or significant head trauma within 3 months; intracranial tumor. Pharmacist move: If eligible, give the lytic within 30 minutes of arrival. Exam trap: BP >180/110 is relative, not absolute.

source.recommendation: 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP ACS guideline: fibrinolytic therapy when timely primary PCI (≤120 min from first medical contact) is not possible, door-to-needle ≤30 min; absolute contraindications include prior ICH, ischemic stroke within 3 months, known intracranial neoplasm/vascular lesion, active bleeding, suspected aortic dissection, significant closed head or facial trauma within 3 months; severe uncontrolled hypertension (>180/110) is relative.

topic: Chronic coronary disease: antianginals, SL nitroglycerin counseling
front: Stable angina patient gets sublingual nitroglycerin. Counsel dose, timing and storage.
bottom: 0.4 mg every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses.

bullets.clue: Call 911 if pain isn't better 5 minutes after the first dose.
bullets.treat: Keep in original glass bottle; long-acting nitrates need a 10–14 h nitrate-free interval.
bullets.trap: No PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates.

back: 0.4 mg every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses. Key clue: Call 911 if pain isn't better 5 minutes after the first dose. Pharmacist move: Keep in original glass bottle; long-acting nitrates need a 10–14 h nitrate-free interval. Exam trap: No PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates.

source.recommendation: 2023 AHA/ACC Chronic Coronary Disease guideline: SL nitroglycerin for immediate relief; beta-blocker or CCB as first-line antianginal. Nitroglycerin SL labeling: 0.4 mg at onset, may repeat every 5 minutes up to 3 doses; seek emergency care if pain persists 5 minutes after first dose; store in original glass container; contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors.

topic: AF: CHA2DS2-VASc and DOAC selection/dose reductions
front: AF patient, 72-year-old woman with hypertension. Anticoagulate? Which drug?
bottom: Yes: CHA2DS2-VASc 3. DOAC over warfarin.

bullets.clue: Age 65–74 (1) + female (1) + hypertension (1) = 3.
bullets.treat: Anticoagulate at ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women; dose DOACs by label criteria.
bullets.trap: Mechanical valve or moderate-severe mitral stenosis: warfarin, not a DOAC.

back: Yes: CHA2DS2-VASc 3. DOAC over warfarin. Key clue: Age 65–74 (1) + female (1) + hypertension (1) = 3. Pharmacist move: Anticoagulate at ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women; dose DOACs by label criteria. Exam trap: Mechanical valve or moderate-severe mitral stenosis: warfarin, not a DOAC.

source.recommendation: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline: anticoagulation recommended for annual stroke risk ≥2% (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 men, ≥3 women); DOACs preferred over warfarin except with mechanical heart valves or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis; dose per label.

topic: AF rate vs rhythm control drug choices
front: AF with rapid rate: what controls rate, and who can take flecainide?
bottom: Rate: beta-blocker or diltiazem/verapamil.

bullets.clue: Avoid non-DHP CCBs in HFrEF.
bullets.treat: Flecainide or propafenone only without structural heart disease; add an AV nodal blocker.
bullets.trap: HFrEF rhythm control: amiodarone or dofetilide; ablation is often first-line.

back: Rate: beta-blocker or diltiazem/verapamil. Key clue: Avoid non-DHP CCBs in HFrEF. Pharmacist move: Flecainide or propafenone only without structural heart disease; add an AV nodal blocker. Exam trap: HFrEF rhythm control: amiodarone or dofetilide; ablation is often first-line.

source.recommendation: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline: rate control with beta-blockers or non-DHP CCBs (avoid non-DHP CCBs with LVEF <40%); class IC drugs (flecainide, propafenone) only without structural heart disease/ischemic heart disease, used with AV nodal blockade; amiodarone or dofetilide in HFrEF; catheter ablation first-line in selected patients including HFrEF.

topic: VTE treatment & duration; DOAC vs warfarin; cancer VTE
front: Provoked DVT treated with apixaban. Dose, and how long?
bottom: 10 mg BID for 7 days, then 5 mg BID; 3 months.

bullets.clue: Rivaroxaban: 15 mg BID for 21 days, then 20 mg daily with food.
bullets.treat: Dabigatran and edoxaban need 5–10 days of parenteral lead-in.
bullets.trap: Unprovoked VTE: reassess for extended therapy after 3 months.

back: 10 mg BID for 7 days, then 5 mg BID; 3 months. Key clue: Rivaroxaban: 15 mg BID for 21 days, then 20 mg daily with food. Pharmacist move: Dabigatran and edoxaban need 5–10 days of parenteral lead-in. Exam trap: Unprovoked VTE: reassess for extended therapy after 3 months.

source.guideline: CHEST 2021 VTE (2024 compendium); 2026 AHA/ACC multisociety acute PE guideline
source.recommendation: CHEST 2021 VTE: DOACs over VKA; 3 months for VTE provoked by transient risk factor; extended therapy for unprovoked VTE in many patients; cancer-associated VTE—apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban. 2026 AHA/ACC acute PE guideline: DOAC over warfarin when appropriate. Dosing per labeling (apixaban 10 mg BID × 7 days then 5 mg BID; rivaroxaban 15 mg BID × 21 days then 20 mg daily with food; dabigatran/edoxaban after 5–10 days parenteral anticoagulation).

topic: VTE prophylaxis in hospitalized patients
front: Acutely ill medical inpatient, low bleeding risk. VTE prophylaxis pick?
bottom: LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin 40 mg daily) over UFH.

bullets.clue: High bleeding risk: mechanical prophylaxis instead.
bullets.treat: Stop at discharge; don't routinely extend.
bullets.trap: ASH prefers LMWH over DOACs for inpatient medical prophylaxis.

back: LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin 40 mg daily) over UFH. Key clue: High bleeding risk: mechanical prophylaxis instead. Pharmacist move: Stop at discharge; don't routinely extend. Exam trap: ASH prefers LMWH over DOACs for inpatient medical prophylaxis.

source.recommendation: ASH 2018 VTE prophylaxis in medical patients: pharmacological prophylaxis with LMWH (preferred over UFH) for acutely ill medical patients; mechanical prophylaxis when bleeding risk high; against extended-duration prophylaxis after discharge; against DOACs for inpatient prophylaxis.

topic: HIT: stop heparin, argatroban/bivalirudin
front: Platelets fell 60% on day 6 of heparin with a new clot. What now?
bottom: Suspected HIT: stop all heparin.

bullets.clue: 4Ts score; includes LMWH and heparin flushes.
bullets.treat: Start a non-heparin anticoagulant: argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or a DOAC.
bullets.trap: Don't start warfarin until platelets recover (≥150k); reverse warfarin with vitamin K if already on it.

back: Suspected HIT: stop all heparin. Key clue: 4Ts score; includes LMWH and heparin flushes. Pharmacist move: Start a non-heparin anticoagulant: argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or a DOAC. Exam trap: Don't start warfarin until platelets recover (≥150k); reverse warfarin with vitamin K if already on it.

diagram.alt: HIT algorithm: platelet fall over 50 percent at day 5 to 10 or new clot, calculate 4Ts; if intermediate or high, stop all heparin including flushes and LMWH, start a non-heparin anticoagulant, send the PF4 test; delay warfarin until platelets are at least 150,000 and give vitamin K if already on warfarin.

source.recommendation: ASH 2018 HIT guideline: stop all heparin when HIT suspected (intermediate/high 4Ts); start non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, danaparoid, fondaparinux, DOAC); do not start VKA until platelet recovery (usually ≥150 × 10⁹/L); give vitamin K if on VKA at diagnosis; avoid platelet transfusion unless bleeding.

topic: ACLS drugs: epinephrine, amiodarone, adenosine, atropine
front: Pulseless VF after 2 shocks. Which drugs and doses?
bottom: Epinephrine 1 mg every 3–5 minutes.

bullets.clue: Refractory VF/pVT: amiodarone 300 mg, then 150 mg (or lidocaine).
bullets.treat: Stable SVT: adenosine 6 mg rapid push, then 12 mg. Bradycardia: atropine 1 mg, max 3 mg.
bullets.trap: Vasopressin isn't in the adult arrest algorithm.

back: Epinephrine 1 mg every 3–5 minutes. Key clue: Refractory VF/pVT: amiodarone 300 mg, then 150 mg (or lidocaine). Pharmacist move: Stable SVT: adenosine 6 mg rapid push, then 12 mg. Bradycardia: atropine 1 mg, max 3 mg. Exam trap: Vasopressin isn't in the adult arrest algorithm.

diagram.alt: Adult cardiac arrest, shockable rhythm: CPR and shock, epinephrine 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes after the second shock, amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock then 150 mg, or lidocaine 1 to 1.5 mg/kg then 0.5 to 0.75 mg/kg.

source.recommendation: AHA 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC: epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 minutes; amiodarone 300 mg then 150 mg or lidocaine for shock-refractory VF/pVT; adenosine 6 mg then 12 mg for stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia; atropine 1 mg every 3–5 minutes up to 3 mg for symptomatic bradycardia.

topic: PAD: antiplatelet, cilostazol (HF contraindication), rivaroxaban 2.5
front: PAD with claudication and HFrEF: antithrombotics, and can you add cilostazol?
bottom: No cilostazol: contraindicated in heart failure.

bullets.clue: Single antiplatelet (aspirin or clopidogrel) for symptomatic PAD.
bullets.treat: Consider rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BID plus aspirin; high-intensity statin; supervised exercise.
bullets.trap: Cilostazol boxed warning covers HF of any severity.

back: No cilostazol: contraindicated in heart failure. Key clue: Single antiplatelet (aspirin or clopidogrel) for symptomatic PAD. Pharmacist move: Consider rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BID plus aspirin; high-intensity statin; supervised exercise. Exam trap: Cilostazol boxed warning covers HF of any severity.

source.recommendation: 2024 ACC/AHA multisociety PAD guideline: single antiplatelet therapy for symptomatic PAD; low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BID plus aspirin to reduce MACE/MALE; high-intensity statin; cilostazol for claudication; supervised exercise. Cilostazol labeling: contraindicated in heart failure of any severity (boxed warning).

topic: T2D: metformin plus GLP-1 RA/SGLT2i by comorbidity
front: T2D with HFrEF and CKD, A1c 7.2% on metformin. Add what?
bottom: SGLT2 inhibitor, regardless of A1c.

bullets.clue: ASCVD: GLP-1 RA or SGLT2i with proven benefit.
bullets.treat: Obesity: GLP-1 RA or tirzepatide for weight; CKD: SGLT2i plus consider GLP-1 RA.
bullets.trap: Cardiorenal benefit is independent of A1c and metformin use.

back: SGLT2 inhibitor, regardless of A1c. Key clue: ASCVD: GLP-1 RA or SGLT2i with proven benefit. Pharmacist move: Obesity: GLP-1 RA or tirzepatide for weight; CKD: SGLT2i plus consider GLP-1 RA. Exam trap: Cardiorenal benefit is independent of A1c and metformin use.

source.recommendation: ADA Standards of Care 2026 (Section 9): in T2D with HF or CKD, SGLT2i with demonstrated benefit; with ASCVD, GLP-1 RA and/or SGLT2i with demonstrated CV benefit; independent of A1c and metformin; GLP-1 RA or dual GIP/GLP-1 RA for weight management.

topic: T2D A1c goals and individualization; older adults
front: A1c goal for a healthy 50-year-old vs a frail 82-year-old with falls?
bottom: Most adults <7%; frail older adults <8% or looser.

bullets.clue: Hypoglycemia risk, comorbidities and life expectancy drive the goal.
bullets.treat: Deintensify insulin and sulfonylureas when hypoglycemia outweighs benefit.
bullets.trap: Tighter isn't better when it causes hypoglycemia.

back: Most adults <7%; frail older adults <8% or looser. Key clue: Hypoglycemia risk, comorbidities and life expectancy drive the goal. Pharmacist move: Deintensify insulin and sulfonylureas when hypoglycemia outweighs benefit. Exam trap: Tighter isn't better when it causes hypoglycemia.

source.recommendation: ADA Standards of Care 2026 (Sections 6 and 13): A1c <7% for many nonpregnant adults without significant hypoglycemia; less stringent goals (e.g., <8.0%) for older adults with complex health; deintensify hypoglycemia-causing agents in older adults.

topic: Insulin initiation and titration (basal 10 U or 0.1–0.2 U/kg)
front: Starting basal insulin in T2D. Dose and titration?
bottom: 10 units or 0.1–0.2 units/kg daily.

bullets.clue: Titrate 2–4 units (or 10–15%) once or twice weekly to fasting 80–130.
bullets.treat: Watch for overbasalization: basal >0.5 units/kg, bedtime-to-morning drop.
bullets.trap: Above 0.5 units/kg: add prandial insulin or GLP-1 RA instead of more basal.

back: 10 units or 0.1–0.2 units/kg daily. Key clue: Titrate 2–4 units (or 10–15%) once or twice weekly to fasting 80–130. Pharmacist move: Watch for overbasalization: basal >0.5 units/kg, bedtime-to-morning drop. Exam trap: Above 0.5 units/kg: add prandial insulin or GLP-1 RA instead of more basal.

source.recommendation: ADA Standards of Care 2026 (Section 9): start basal insulin 10 units/day or 0.1–0.2 units/kg/day; adjust 10–15% or 2–4 units once or twice weekly to fasting target (typical 80–130 mg/dL); overbasalization signs include basal dose >0.5 units/kg/day, high bedtime-to-morning differential, hypoglycemia; consider GLP-1 RA or prandial insulin.

topic: Hypoglycemia: rule of 15, glucagon forms
front: Glucose 58 mg/dL, patient awake. Treatment, and when is glucagon needed?
bottom: 15 g fast carbs, recheck in 15 minutes.

bullets.clue: Level 1 <70; level 2 <54; level 3 needs assistance.
bullets.treat: Unable to swallow: glucagon (nasal 3 mg or injection); prescribe it for insulin users.
bullets.trap: On acarbose, use glucose tablets: sucrose won't absorb fast.

back: 15 g fast carbs, recheck in 15 minutes. Key clue: Level 1 <70; level 2 <54; level 3 needs assistance. Pharmacist move: Unable to swallow: glucagon (nasal 3 mg or injection); prescribe it for insulin users. Exam trap: On acarbose, use glucose tablets: sucrose won't absorb fast.

source.recommendation: ADA Standards of Care 2026 (Section 6): treat glucose <70 mg/dL with 15–20 g glucose, recheck in 15 min and repeat if needed; glucagon prescribed for those at risk of level 2 or 3 hypoglycemia. Acarbose labeling: treat hypoglycemia with glucose (dextrose), not sucrose.

topic: DKA/HHS: fluids, insulin, potassium thresholds
front: DKA with potassium 3.1. Start the insulin drip?
bottom: No: replace potassium first; start insulin at K ≥3.5.

bullets.clue: Fluids first: isotonic crystalloid 1–1.5 L in the first hour.
bullets.treat: Insulin 0.1 units/kg/h; add dextrose when glucose falls below 250.
bullets.trap: Give SC basal insulin about 2 hours before stopping the drip.

back: No: replace potassium first; start insulin at K ≥3.5. Key clue: Fluids first: isotonic crystalloid 1–1.5 L in the first hour. Pharmacist move: Insulin 0.1 units/kg/h; add dextrose when glucose falls below 250. Exam trap: Give SC basal insulin about 2 hours before stopping the drip.

diagram.alt: DKA potassium gate: fluids first, 1 to 1.5 L isotonic crystalloid in hour one. Potassium below 3.5: hold insulin and replace potassium. 3.5 to 5: insulin 0.1 units/kg/h plus potassium in fluids. Above 5: insulin, no potassium, recheck. Add dextrose when glucose falls below 250; basal insulin about 2 hours before stopping the drip.

source.recommendation: 2024 ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS hyperglycemic crises consensus: isotonic crystalloid 1–1.5 L first hour; hold insulin if K <3.5 mmol/L and replace potassium; IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/h; add dextrose 5–10% when glucose <250 mg/dL; give SC basal insulin 1–2 h before stopping IV insulin (ADA Standards of Care 2026: 2 h).

topic: GLP-1 RA/GIP: adverse effects, pancreatitis, gastroparesis, obesity dosing
front: Starting semaglutide for weight: counseling on side effects and titration?
bottom: Slow titration limits GI effects.

bullets.clue: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation; gallbladder disease; pancreatitis.
bullets.treat: Stop and seek care for severe abdominal pain; don't combine with a DPP-4 inhibitor.
bullets.trap: Boxed warning: no use with personal or family MTC or MEN 2.

back: Slow titration limits GI effects. Key clue: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation; gallbladder disease; pancreatitis. Pharmacist move: Stop and seek care for severe abdominal pain; don't combine with a DPP-4 inhibitor. Exam trap: Boxed warning: no use with personal or family MTC or MEN 2.

source.recommendation: Semaglutide (Wegovy) labeling: dose escalation every 4 weeks to 2.4 mg weekly to reduce GI adverse reactions; warnings for acute pancreatitis, gallbladder disease; boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors. ADA Standards 2026: avoid combining GLP-1 RA with DPP-4 inhibitors.

topic: Hypothyroidism: levothyroxine dosing, TSH timing, administration
front: New levothyroxine for an 80-year-old with CAD. Starting dose, administration and follow-up?
bottom: Start low: 12.5–50 mcg daily.

bullets.clue: Healthy younger adults: about 1.6 mcg/kg/day.
bullets.treat: Empty stomach 30–60 minutes before breakfast; recheck TSH in 6–8 weeks.
bullets.trap: Separate from calcium and iron by 4 hours.

back: Start low: 12.5–50 mcg daily. Key clue: Healthy younger adults: about 1.6 mcg/kg/day. Pharmacist move: Empty stomach 30–60 minutes before breakfast; recheck TSH in 6–8 weeks. Exam trap: Separate from calcium and iron by 4 hours.

source.guideline: ATA 2014 hypothyroidism (still current, latest = 2014); ATA 2026 pregnancy guideline
source.recommendation: ATA 2014 hypothyroidism guideline: full replacement ~1.6 mcg/kg/day; lower starting dose in elderly or CAD (e.g., 12.5–50 mcg); take on empty stomach 60 min before breakfast (or at bedtime 3 h after meal); TSH 6–8 weeks after dose change. Levothyroxine labeling: separate from calcium/iron by ≥4 hours.

topic: Hyperthyroidism: methimazole vs PTU (pregnancy T1)
front: Graves' disease: which antithyroid drug normally, and which in early pregnancy?
bottom: Methimazole usually; PTU until 16 weeks of pregnancy.

bullets.clue: Switch methimazole to PTU as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.

back: Methimazole usually; PTU until 16 weeks of pregnancy. Key clue: Switch methimazole to PTU as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. Pharmacist move: Counsel: fever or sore throat on either drug means a CBC for agranulocytosis. Exam trap: PTU has a boxed warning for severe liver injury.

source.guideline: ATA 2016 hyperthyroidism; ATA 2026 pregnancy/postpartum thyroid guideline
source.recommendation: ATA 2016 hyperthyroidism guideline: methimazole preferred except first trimester of pregnancy, thyroid storm, or methimazole intolerance; obtain CBC for fever/sore throat (agranulocytosis). ATA 2026 pregnancy/postpartum guideline: switch from methimazole to PTU (1:20 ratio) as soon as pregnancy confirmed if PTU available; treat with PTU until 16 weeks; consider stopping ATDs in low-risk women. PTU labeling: boxed warning for severe liver injury.
